column2: CH14 Q1: Row-Level Security Design Principles
Select ALL that apply: An organization is designing row-level security for a multi-tenant application. Which principles should guide the design?

column3: Each authenticated user should only access rows belonging to their own organization or account
column5: Correct - this is the core principle of multi-tenant RLS.

column3: A service account with broad access should be embedded in public browser code for convenience
column5: Incorrect - broad credentials must never be exposed in public code.

column3: AI retrieval systems should respect the same row-level permissions as direct user access
column5: Correct - AI does not create an exception to privacy rules.

column3: An instructor role should have different row access than a student role
column5: Correct - role-based access is a fundamental RLS pattern.

column3: Row-level policies act like automatic WHERE conditions added to relevant queries
column5: Correct - this is the conceptual model for how RLS policies work.
Think about least privilege - who needs access to what, and how should that be enforced?

Row-level security applies authorization at the row level. Policies act as automatic WHERE clauses. Different roles need different access. AI retrieval must respect the same permissions. Service credentials must never be exposed publicly.

column2: Select ALL that apply: A hospital wants to use AI to answer staff questions using approved policy documents. Which architecture decisions support responsible implementation?

column3: Store policy documents with version numbers, effective dates, and approval status
column5: Correct - versioned, dated, and approved documents are essential for AI readiness.

column3: Create retrieval views that expose only approved and current document versions
column5: Correct - governed views prevent stale or draft content from reaching the model.

column3: Apply row-level or document-level access controls before retrieval
column5: Correct - authorization must occur before data enters the model context.

column3: Allow the AI model to access all documents in the network without restriction
column5: Incorrect - unrestricted access violates privacy and governance principles.

column3: Include source citations and effective dates in generated answers
column5: Correct - citations allow users to verify the source and check currency.
Authorization must happen before data reaches the model. What metadata and controls make retrieval trustworthy?

AI-ready document systems require version control, approval status, effective dates, governed retrieval views, pre-retrieval access controls, and citations. Unrestricted access is a dangerous anti-pattern.

column3: Maintain the registration system on an OLTP-optimized database and periodically load cleaned grade history into a separate analytical store

Think about what happens when a complex historical query runs against a live transaction system.
OLTP and OLAP have different design priorities. Separating them preserves transaction speed for operations while enabling historical analysis without disruption.

column2: An organization built a data warehouse three years ago. Two departments now report different values for monthly revenue even though both use the same warehouse. What is the most likely root cause?

column3: The warehouse hardware is faulty
column5: Incorrect - The warehouse hardware is faulty

column3: The organization lacks a single governed definition of the metric, and departments apply different filters or inclusion rules
column5: Correct - The organization lacks a single governed definition of the metric, and departmen

column3: SQL cannot calculate revenue correctly
column5: Incorrect - SQL cannot calculate revenue correctly

column3: One department is using OLTP instead of OLAP
column5: Incorrect - One department is using OLTP instead of OLAP
When different people get different answers from the same data, what is usually missing?

Conflicting numbers from the same source typically indicate a governance gap - no single agreed-upon definition of the metric. Without governance, different filters and rules produce different results.

column3: Document columns are incompatible with modern databases
column5: Incorrect - Document columns are incompatible with modern databases

column3: Flexibility without governance leads to inconsistency - the documents lack enforced naming conventions and validation
column5: Correct - Flexibility without governance leads to inconsistency - the documents lack enfor

column3: The data should have been stored in a graph database
column5: Incorrect - The data should have been stored in a graph database

column3: Document columns cannot store numeric values

The problem is not the technology - it is how the technology is being used without rules.
Flexible document storage offers adaptability, but flexibility without governance creates chaos. Without naming conventions and validation, the same concept gets recorded under different names.

column2: A bank's distributed transaction system experiences a network partition between two data centers. Customer account balances are at stake. Which CAP trade-off decision is most defensible?

column3: Prioritize availability - allow both centers to process withdrawals independently, accepting potential inconsistency
column5: Incorrect - Prioritize availability - allow both centers to process withdrawals independentl

column3: Prioritize consistency - suspend transactions at one center until communication is restored, protecting balance accuracy
column5: Correct - Prioritize consistency - suspend transactions at one center until communication

column3: Shut down all banking operations globally until the network is fixed
column5: Incorrect - Shut down all banking operations globally until the network is fixed

column3: Ignore the partition and hope it resolves itself
column5: Incorrect - Ignore the partition and hope it resolves itself
What is worse for a bank: temporarily declining some transactions, or allowing accounts to be overdrawn?
For financial transactions, consistency is more important than availability. The CAP theorem states you cannot have both during a partition - you must choose. Banking prioritizes correctness.

column2: CH14 Q7: Prompt Is Not a Security Boundary

A company is building a customer-facing AI assistant. The proposed architecture sends the entire customer database to the LLM with every request, relying on a prompt instruction to limit access. What is the most serious flaw?

column3: The prompt is too long for the LLM to process
column5: Incorrect - The prompt is too long for the LLM to process

column3: Using a prompt instruction as a security boundary is not reliable - authorization must be enforced through database controls before data reaches the model
column5: Correct - Using a prompt instruction as a security boundary is not reliable - authorizatio

column3: LLMs cannot process database records
column5: Incorrect - LLMs cannot process database records

column3: The database should use NoSQL instead
column5: Incorrect - The database should use NoSQL instead
Can you trust a language model to reliably enforce access control through natural language instructions?

A prompt instruction is not a security boundary. Authorization must be enforced through database access controls before data reaches the model. Sending all data and hoping the model filters correctly is dangerous.

column5: Incorrect - Continue with the current approach - performance will improve automatically

column3: Evaluate which fields are consistently queried and consider extracting them into indexed relational columns while keeping truly variable attributes in documents
column5: Correct - Evaluate which fields are consistently queried and consider extracting them into

The chapter recommends a specific pattern: a relational core with a flexible edge.

A hybrid approach is best: keep stable, frequently-queried fields in indexed relational columns, and use document columns for truly variable attributes. This preserves flexibility while gaining relational performance.

column2: CH14 Q9: RAG - Retrieval vs. Generation Failure
A RAG system retrieves a policy document and generates an answer. The answer is fluent but contradicts the retrieved document. What is the most likely explanation?

column3: The database connection failed
column5: Incorrect - The database connection failed

column3: The model generated a plausible continuation not faithful to the evidence - retrieval succeeded but generation failed
column5: Correct - The model generated a plausible continuation not faithful to the evidence - retr

column3: Vector search cannot retrieve text documents
column5: Incorrect - Vector search cannot retrieve text documents

column3: The user asked the wrong question
column5: Incorrect - The user asked the wrong question
RAG has two stages. If the right document was found but the answer is wrong, which stage failed?

RAG can fail at retrieval (wrong documents) or generation (model ignores evidence). When the correct document was retrieved but the answer contradicts it, generation failed - the model produced fluent but unfaithful output.

column2: CH14 Q10: Relational Relevance for Modern Workloads

The chapter argues that modern infrastructure does not always require abandoning relational databases. A growing company with operational, analytical, and AI retrieval needs should consider which approach?

column3: Replace everything with a vector database for AI workloads
column5: Incorrect - Replace everything with a vector database for AI workloads

column3: A strong relational platform can support all three modes - operational, analytical, and AI retrieval - when the workload and scale are appropriate
column5: Correct - A strong relational platform can support all three modes - operational, analytic

column3: Relational databases are obsolete for any modern use case
column5: Incorrect - Relational databases are obsolete for any modern use case

column3: Use separate NoSQL systems for each mode with no relational component
column5: Incorrect - Use separate NoSQL systems for each mode with no relational component
Reread the chapter's central thesis about what changes and what remains at scale.

The chapter's central thesis: relational databases remain foundational. Modern platforms support operational tables, analytical queries, document columns, full-text search, and vector similarity - all within one environment.
